subject: Bressman et al. (1994)
object: Bressman et al. (1994) examined 53 individuals from 4 generations of a non-Jewish North American family with adult-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia. Seven family members were affected, with a mean age at onset of 28.4 years (range, 7 to 50 years). In 6 of the 7, the neck was affected first; all 7 developed cervical dystonia, and 5 had dysarthria or dysphonia.

subject: Bressman et al. (1994)
object: Bressman et al. (1994) found that linkage data excluded the DYT1 region on chromosome 9q34 in this non-Jewish family with adult cervical-onset dystonia. They concluded that a gene other than DYT1 is responsible for some cases of adult cervical-onset dystonia.

subject: Fuchs et al. (2013)
object: Fuchs et al. (2013) used exome sequencing in 2 families with autosomal dominant primary torsion dystonia (PTD) and found heterozygous mutations in the GNAL gene in both: a nonsense mutation (S293X) in family P, located within one of 3 regions of potential linkage (LOD scores 1.5 to 2.1), and a missense mutation (V137M) in family D1. Sanger sequencing of the GNAL coding region in 39 additional multiplex PTD families of mixed European origin who were negative for DYT1 and DYT6 mutations identified 6 additional novel mutations in 6 families (19%). Segregation with disease was confirmed in all families with DNA from multiple affected individuals, and none of the variants was found in dbSNP135, about 3,500 European exomes, or 572 control chromosomes.

subject: Fuchs et al. (2013)
object: Fuchs et al. (2013) described 28 individuals with definite dystonia from 8 multiplex families with GNAL mutations, all Caucasian of mixed European ancestry. Mean age at onset was 31.3 years (range, 7 to 54 years); onset was in the neck in 82%, and 93% had neck involvement at final examination, but most progressed to other sites and only 46% had focal dystonia at last examination. Cranial involvement was present in 57% and speech involvement in 44%; brachial onset was not observed and arm involvement occurred in only 32%, distinguishing the disorder from DYT6.

subject: Fuchs et al. (2013)
object: Fuchs et al. (2013) summarized the phenotype in the 8 GNAL families as predominantly cervical dystonia with a relatively broad range of age at onset and spread to other muscles, especially facial muscles, in over half of subjects. Some individuals had generalized dystonia with leg onset, and other onset sites included larynx, jaw, and tongue.

subject: Fuchs et al. (2013)
object: In affected members of family P with primary torsion dystonia (previously reported; mixed Russian and Swiss Mennonite heritage), Fuchs et al. (2013) identified a heterozygous c.878C>A nonsense mutation in the GNAL gene, resulting in a ser293-to-ter (S293X) substitution. The mutation was found by exome sequencing, co-segregated with dystonia in the family, and was not present in about 3,500 European exomes. In a BRET assay, the S293X mutant failed to support any D1R-driven responses.

subject: Fuchs et al. (2013)
object: In affected members of family D1 with primary torsion dystonia, Fuchs et al. (2013) identified a heterozygous c.409G>A missense mutation in the GNAL gene, resulting in a val137-to-met (V137M) substitution at a residue completely conserved in GNAL orthologs. The mutation was found by exome sequencing, segregated with disease, and was not found in 572 control chromosomes or about 3,500 European exomes. In BRET assays the mutant showed an intermediate phenotype largely consistent with impaired association with Gbeta-gamma subunits.

subject: Fuchs et al. (2013)
object: In 2 affected members of family S with primary torsion dystonia, Fuchs et al. (2013) identified a heterozygous c.463G>A missense mutation in the GNAL gene, resulting in a glu155-to-lys (E155K) substitution at a residue completely conserved in GNAL orthologs. In BRET assays, the mutant showed an intermediate phenotype largely consistent with impaired association with Gbeta-gamma subunits.

subject: Fuchs et al. (2013)
object: In 4 affected members of family D2 with primary torsion dystonia, Fuchs et al. (2013) identified a heterozygous 1-bp insertion (c.283-284insT) in the GNAL gene, resulting in a frameshift and premature termination (S95fsX110), predicted to cause loss of function.

subject: Fuchs et al. (2013)
object: In 3 affected members of family H with primary torsion dystonia, Fuchs et al. (2013) identified a heterozygous 1-bp insertion (c.591-592insA) in the GNAL gene, resulting in a frameshift and premature termination (R198fsX210), predicted to cause loss of function.

subject: Fuchs et al. (2013)
object: In 3 affected members of family T with primary torsion dystonia, Fuchs et al. (2013) identified a heterozygous c.61C>T nonsense mutation in the GNAL gene, resulting in an arg21-to-ter (R21X) substitution, which they predicted to be degraded by nonsense-mediated decay and produce no protein.

subject: Fuchs et al. (2013)
object: In the proband of family N with primary torsion dystonia, Fuchs et al. (2013) identified a heterozygous 9-bp deletion (c.304-312delCCTCCAGTT) in the GNAL gene, resulting in an in-frame deletion of 3 amino acids (P102-V104del).

subject: Fuchs et al. (2013)
object: In 2 affected members of family B with primary torsion dystonia, Fuchs et al. (2013) identified a heterozygous possible splice site mutation (c.274-5T>C; chr18:11,753,820, hg19) upstream of exon 4 of the GNAL gene. Bioinformatic analysis suggested the wildtype sequence was 10 times more likely than the mutant to be found near an acceptor splice site, but the effect could not be proven because GNAL expression was undetectable in patient lymphoblasts.

subject: Fuchs et al. (2013)
object: Using a cell-based BRET assay in HEK293 cells in which Galpha-olf function is assessed by its interaction with Gbeta-gamma subunits during the D1 dopamine receptor-initiated cycle, Fuchs et al. (2013) found that the S293X mutant failed to support any D1R-driven responses, E155K and V137M showed intermediate impairment, and the control variant V16F behaved like wildtype. They concluded that the functional assay was suggestive of loss of function, and that GNAL mutations point to primary abnormalities of D1R and/or A2AR transmission in striatal neurons as possibly leading to dystonia.

subject: Fuchs et al. (2013)
object: Fuchs et al. (2013) noted that dystonia was inherited in an autosomal dominant manner in the GNAL families. Because GNAL may be imprinted, they examined parental origin and found that dystonia was inherited equally from maternal and paternal sides, with no apparent phenotypic differences between maternally and paternally inherited cases.

subject: Fuchs et al. (2013)
object: Fuchs et al. (2013) found no genotype/phenotype correlation with regard to mutation type, and phenotypes varied within families carrying the same GNAL mutation.

subject: Fuchs et al. (2013)
object: Fuchs et al. (2013) noted that GNAL is located on chromosome 18p, centromeric to the DYT7 and DYT15 loci, and that dystonia occurs in patients with 18p deletions, suggesting that absence of GNAL may contribute to dystonia in these cases.
